clarification_questions.question: What goes wrong today with carcass grading by fat content, and what decision should the real-time data drive on the line?
clarification_questions.why: Defines the decision and whether a sensor is the right answer.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Decision and current grading practice unknown; the feasibility plan starts with clarifying the grading decision.

clarification_questions.question: What fat content levels and range must be distinguished for grading, and is this expressed as a percentage of the carcass or otherwise?
clarification_questions.why: Sets the concentration level and whether the method's sensitivity is sufficient.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Fat level unknown; lab screening establishes the concentration level and grading resolution required.

clarification_questions.question: What is the carcass surface like at measurement (skin, feathers, moisture, color, cut surface) and how much does it vary between carcasses?
clarification_questions.why: Surface state and variability decide whether ATR contact or another optical geometry is workable.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Surface condition unknown; lab screening on representative carcass surfaces is needed before any probe choice.

clarification_questions.question: What are the line conditions: conveyor speed, cleaning or sanitation regime, and temperature or humidity at the measuring point?
clarification_questions.why: Speed and cleaning determine whether contact-based ATR is feasible and how fouling affects the probe.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Line conditions unknown; in-line trial design cannot be fixed until they are known.

clarification_questions.question: What is the planned distance from the probe to the carcass and would the carcass touch the probe face?
clarification_questions.why: Contact or stand-off distance determines whether ATR, diffuse reflection or another geometry applies.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Contact and distance unknown; the paper's ATR configuration cannot be assumed to transfer to a conveyor.

clarification_questions.question: What reference method is used today to determine fat content, and what is its accuracy?
clarification_questions.why: A reference is required to show whether any sensor agrees with lab practice.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Reference method unknown; no accuracy comparison is possible until it is provided.

clarification_questions.question: What accuracy, response time and budget are required for the grading system, and what does 'validated' need to mean for your customers?
clarification_questions.why: Defines acceptance criteria and whether a validation claim can be supported.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Requirements unknown; no validation claim can be made until acceptance criteria and evidence are agreed.

flags_before_revision.detail: different_context: The paper uses IR to discriminate fat in lab chicken tissue samples; the claim says 'the MIR signal separated fat', which is accurate for that context, but the source says fat discrimination was partial and PCA on IR alone did not fully separate the classes. Stating it as separation overstates the result. Fix: Say that in the lab study, IR spectroscopy worked better than fluorescence for discriminating fat, but did not fully separate the three tissue classes on its own.

not_supported: The cited pages do not state that ATR requires tight contact and a micrometre-scale depth while excluding stand-off mounting; the S01 p.6 table gives ATR depth of 1-6 um, but the claim that stand-off mounting over a conveyor does not match the principle is an inference not stated in the sources (and the NIR rows are cited as if they were ATR evidence). Fix: Limit the claim to the cited table values: ATR platform/probe rows list optical depth 1-6 um and liquid, paste, soft samples; state the contact requirement only as the S04 p.4 'tight contact with the probe head' statement.

not_supported: S01 p.17 describes inline NIR reflection for opaque dairy products such as yogurt, butter and whole milk concentrates. It does not say fat in opaque food is measured or that the method can measure without contact; the non-contact statement is from S01 p.10 about NIR at a distance, and it refers to probe-based diffuse reflection flush-mounted in a pipe, which is contact with the flow. Fix: Cite the dairy example as a reflection probe flush-mounted into a pipe or vat for opaque dairy products, and cite S01 p.10 separately for the general at-a-distance diffuse reflectance capability.

overstated: The S04 p.4 text says IR works better for fat discrimination in the lab chicken study; it does not identify the ester carbonyl band as the separating feature in that claim (that is at p.3), and it does not say the separation was complete. Fix: Quote the p.4 statement and note that the ester carbonyl band near 1740 cm-1 (S04 p.3) is the basis, while acknowledging that IR alone did not fully separate the classes.

not_supported: S02 p.6 lists Vis-NIR silica fibers as 350-2400 nm, which covers the NIR range 780-2500 nm only partially, and the chalcogenide and polycrystalline fibers as covering MIR partially; the 'MIR needs' wording turns partial coverage into a requirement that the figure does not state. Fix: State that Vis-NIR silica fibers cover only part of the NIR range listed on S02 p.6, and that the figure lists chalcogenide (1.1-6.5 um) and polycrystalline (3-17 um) fibers for the infrared range.

overstated: The fiber coverage classification (full versus partial) is the model's own rule and is not stated on S02 p.6, which only gives approximate transmission ranges; calling the coverage full or partial for NIR and MIR is an interpretation presented as a source fact. Fix: Present the fiber ranges as approximate values from S02 p.6 and mark the full/partial classification as an interpretation to be checked against the figure and the actual fiber specification.

not_supported: S01 p.7 discusses synergy of combined spectral methods in general and gives examples of successful combinations; it does not state that NIR or a method combination is not guaranteed to grade adequately. The claim reframes a general synergy statement as a risk statement with a different meaning. Fix: Cite S01 p.7 only for the statement that combinations can give synergy in some problems, and state the grading risk as an assumption to test rather than a source finding.

RAMAN.nominal_range: Raman shift in cm-1; signal recorded in the visible / short-wave NIR (400-1100 nm); state the laser excitation separately [S01 p.11]

FLUO.nominal_range: UV/Vis excitation and emission; depends on the fluorescent species [S01 p.12]

UVVIS.nominal_range: UV 190-360 nm and visible; depends on target and setup [S01 p.5]

rule_hints: fluorescence_needs_fluorophore: Fluorescence only measures a defined fluorescent species or a justified indicator; most chemicals do not fluoresce. [S01 p.5; S04 p.4; DOCX §5]
sensitivity_not_selectivity: High sensitivity does not imply selectivity. Fluorimetry and UV/Vis are rated high sensitivity but low selectivity. [S01 Table 1 (p.6); DOCX §5]
nominal_range_not_instrument_range: A nominal method range is not the usable range of a specific instrument, fiber or probe. [DOCX §3; DOCX §5]
combination_is_hypothesis: Combining methods can add complementary information, but the gain is a hypothesis to test against the best single method. [S01 p.7-8; DOCX §5]

fiber_limits_wavelength: The fiber determines which wavelengths reach the probe. Silica fibers transmit up to about 2.4 um and cannot carry mid-IR; mid-IR needs chalcogenide, polycrystalline or hollow-waveguide fibers. [S02 p.6; S04 p.1; DOCX §5]
remote_measurement_nir_silica: NIR works with standard glass optics and silica fibers, which suits remote online measurement; robust silica cables of 100-300 m exist. [S01 p.5; S02 p.7]
do_not_invent: Do not invent measured results, accuracy, detection limits, response times, fiber lengths, product codes or prices, client facts, or guarantees. [DOCX §3]
